name: Usable Security & Privacy
description: Human factors: user studies, mental models, warnings, and the usability of security and privacy tools.
narrative:
The earliest listed work at USENIX Security in this space was less about controlled lab studies and more about understanding security as a real-world, socially embedded practice. Papers like "Understanding the Reproducibility of Crowd-reported Security Vulnerabilities" (2018) and "How Do Tor Users Interact With Onion Services?" (2018) examined how ordinary people and crowds actually engage with security systems, while "The aftermath of a crypto-ransomware attack at a large academic institution" (2018) used a single organizational incident to surface the human and institutional fallout of an attack. The common thread was treating users, operators, and communities as the unit of analysis rather than the algorithm.

By 2019 the area sharpened into rigorous user studies and at-scale measurement of human behavior. "Understanding and Improving Security and Privacy in Multi-User Smart Homes" (2019) showed that security is fundamentally a multi-user, multi-stakeholder negotiation, while "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting" (2019) demonstrated how warning and notification design could be deployed at internet scale. This period also broadened the lens to vulnerable and at-risk populations, with work on human trafficking survivors and victim service providers (2019), and later "The Tools and Tactics Used in Intimate Partner Surveillance" (2020) and "Collective Information Security in Large-Scale Urban Protests: the Case of Hong Kong" (2021), establishing at-risk users and developers as first-class subjects.

Around 2020-2021 the field matured along two tracks: the usability of developers (not just end users), and careful study of warnings, nudges, and authentication adoption. "Understanding security mistakes developers make" (2020) and "From Needs to Actions to Secure Apps?" (2020) reframed developers as users who need usable tooling, while "Driving 2FA Adoption at Scale" (2021) and "A Large Scale Study of User Behavior, Expectations and Engagement with Android Permissions" (2021) brought experimental rigor to notification and permission design at population scale.

Most recently the area has turned toward mental models of new and AI-driven threats and toward making abstract privacy guarantees legible. "Exploring User Reactions and Mental Models Towards Perceptual Manipulation Attacks in Mixed Reality" (2023) and "DeepPhish: Understanding User Trust Towards Artificially Generated Profiles" (2022) study how people reason about emerging AR/VR and deepfake threats, while "What Are the Chances? Explaining the Epsilon Parameter in Differential Privacy" (2023) tackles the usability of communicating formal privacy notions. "Glaze: Protecting Artists from Style Mimicry by Text-to-Image Models" (2023) marks the field's pivot toward usable, human-centered protective tools against generative-AI harms, showing the area now sits squarely at the intersection of human factors and AI.
